name: Hy-Brâzil

attributes.attribute: a magical island of peace and plenty ruled by Bres, Niamh, or Manannán mac Lir
appeared every seven years, always in the west
drawn on medieval maps as a real island and gave Brazil its name

sources: Löffler, Christa Maria. The Voyage to the Otherworld Island in Early Irish Literature. Salzburg Studies in English Literature. Salzburg: Institut Für Anglistik und Amerikanistik, Universität Salzburg, 1983, 306+.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Hy-Brâzil is an Irish mythological island. The Celts believed that somewhere in the ocean lay a magical island of peace and plenty. A king, Bres, ruled it. At other times a fairy queen, Niamh of the Golden Hair, or the sea god Manannán mac Lir held sway. The island appeared every seven years, usually in a different place, always in the west. Several islands off the west coast of Ireland claimed to be Hy-Brâzil, including Inisbofin off the Galway coast. In 1908 many people said they had spotted the island in the Atlantic off western Ireland, floating where no island had been seen before. Belief in it was strong and long-lasting. Medieval European maps drew it as a real island, usually off Ireland. When European sailors reached South America, they took its rich lands for the mythological land of plenty. That is why a great country there still bears the name Brazil, drawn from the Celtic island. Hy-Brâzil is sometimes conflated with Tir na nOg, the land of youth, and Mag Mell, the plain of delights, but each has its own qualities.
objective: Document Hy-Brâzil, the Celtic island of plenty, and its link to the name Brazil.
key_results: Record the island and its rulers, Bres, Niamh, and Manannán mac Lir.
Note its seven-year appearances and the claims of Irish islands to be it.
